title: Logic and Proofs
tagline: The foundation of mathematical reasoning: mastering propositional logic, predicate logic, and proof techniques that underpin every theorem in computer science.

sections.content:
Logic is the grammar of mathematics — the discipline that determines what it even means for a statement to be true, and what counts as a valid argument. Every time you write an `if` statement, assert a type invariant, design an API contract, or reason about algorithm correctness, you are applying logic whether you recognise it or not. Understanding logic formally gives you a superpower: the ability to know not just that something works, but **why it must work**, under every possible circumstance, with no exceptions.

**Propositional logic** deals with statements (propositions) that are unambiguously either true or false. These statements are combined using logical connectives: NOT (¬), AND (∧), OR (∨), implication (→), and biconditional (↔). Given any assignment of truth values to the atomic propositions, you can mechanically compute the truth value of any compound formula. This mechanical nature is not a limitation — it is the foundation of circuit design, hardware verification, and automated theorem proving.

**Predicate logic** (also called first-order logic) extends propositional logic by adding the ability to talk about individual objects and their properties. Instead of just P and Q, you write P(x) — 'x has property P' — and use quantifiers to make sweeping statements: ∀x (for all x) and ∃x (there exists an x). This lets you express 'every prime greater than 2 is odd', 'there exists an integer with no square root in the rationals', or 'for every sorting algorithm, there exists an input that requires Ω(n log n) comparisons' — the kinds of universal claims that are the bread and butter of computer science theory.

**Proof techniques** are the systematic methods by which we establish that logical statements are true. A **direct proof** chains together known facts using logical inference rules until it arrives at the desired conclusion. **Proof by contradiction** assumes the opposite of what you want to prove and shows that this assumption leads to an impossibility. **Proof by contrapositive** reframes an implication in its logically equivalent contrapositive form, sometimes making a difficult proof straightforward. **Mathematical induction** provides the canonical technique for proving statements about all natural numbers — indispensable for analyzing algorithms and data structures. Mastering these tools does not just help you pass discrete mathematics exams; it fundamentally changes how you reason about programs, protocols, and systems.

sections.title: Logic as a Circuit Board — and Quantifiers as a Dial
sections.content:
Think of propositions as electrical switches: each is either ON (true) or OFF (false). The connectives are wiring patterns. AND is a **series circuit** — current only flows when both switches are on simultaneously. OR is a **parallel circuit** — current flows whenever at least one switch is on. NOT is an **inverter** that flips the signal. Implication (P → Q) is the most counterintuitive: it is a kind of **conditional relay**. The relay only fails — only outputs false — when the condition P is true but the consequence Q is false. If P is false (the condition never activates), the relay never fails, no matter what Q does. This is the 'vacuous truth' of implication, and it is the single most common source of confusion in a first logic course.

Now extend the metaphor to predicate logic. Add a **dial** to each switch. The dial selects which object x from your domain you are testing. ∀x P(x) means: spin the dial to every possible position, and the switch P stays ON every time. ∃x P(x) means: there exists at least one dial position where P is ON. Truth tables enumerate every combination of ON/OFF for the finite set of propositional switches — but when the dial ranges over an infinite domain (all integers, all strings), you cannot enumerate; you must reason. That reasoning is proof.

sections.title: Propositional Logic: Connectives and Truth Tables
sections.content:
The five core connectives and their truth-functional meanings:

- **¬P (NOT P)**: flips true to false and false to true. The simplest connective.
- **P ∧ Q (P AND Q)**: true only when both P and Q are true. One false input makes the whole conjunction false.
- **P ∨ Q (P OR Q)**: true when at least one of P, Q is true. False only when both are false. This is *inclusive* OR — true even when both are true. (Exclusive OR, XOR, is a different connective.)
- **P → Q (P implies Q, 'if P then Q')**: the most important and most confusing connective. It is false only in one case: when P is true and Q is false. In every other case it is true — including when P is false, which gives the vacuously true cases. Equivalently, P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q.
- **P ↔ Q (P if and only if Q)**: true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value. Equivalent to (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P). Used to express necessary and sufficient conditions.

A **truth table** lists every possible combination of truth values for the atomic propositions and computes the formula's value for each. With n distinct propositions, you need 2ⁿ rows. The standard column ordering uses a binary counting pattern: the rightmost column alternates T/F every row, the next alternates every 2 rows, and so on.

Three classifications emerge from examining a formula's truth table. A **tautology** is a formula that is true in every row, regardless of what truth values the atomic propositions take. Classic examples: P ∨ ¬P (the law of excluded middle), P → P, and (P → Q) → (¬Q → ¬P). A **contradiction** (or unsatisfiable formula) is false in every row. The simplest example is P ∧ ¬P — a statement and its negation cannot both hold. A **contingency** is everything in between: true in some rows, false in others. Most interesting propositions are contingencies.

For large n, truth tables become impractical (100 variables would need 2¹⁰⁰ rows — more than atoms in the universe). This is why **logical equivalence laws** and **satisfiability algorithms** (SAT solvers) matter for real-world applications.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["P = true\nQ = false"] --> B["P ∧ Q = false"]
    A --> C["P ∨ Q = true"]
    A --> D["P → Q = FALSE\nOnly false case!"]
    A --> E["P ↔ Q = false"]
    A --> F["¬P = false"]
    G["P = false\nQ = false"] --> H["P → Q = true\nVacuously true"]
    G --> I["P ∨ Q = false"]
    G --> J["P ∧ Q = false"]
sections.caption: Implication P→Q is false only when P=true and Q=false. When P=false, the implication is always vacuously true — a common point of confusion.

sections.title: Logical Equivalences: The Algebraic Laws of Logic
sections.content:
Just as algebra has identities like a(b+c) = ab+ac, propositional logic has **equivalence laws** — pairs of formulas that always have the same truth value regardless of variable assignment. Knowing these laws lets you rewrite and simplify complex formulas without building a truth table.

**De Morgan's Laws** are the most important pair:
- ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q — negating an AND produces an OR of negations
- ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q — negating an OR produces an AND of negations

The mnemonic: when you push a negation through a connective, the connective flips. AND becomes OR, OR becomes AND. De Morgan's laws are used constantly in programming when you want to invert a compound boolean condition: `!(a && b)` becomes `!a || !b`.

**Implication equivalences:**
- P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q (converting implication to disjunction)
- P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P (the **contrapositive** — logically equivalent and often easier to prove)
- P → Q ≢ Q → P (the **converse** — NOT equivalent; this is a very common logical fallacy)
- P → Q ≢ ¬P → ¬Q (the **inverse** — also NOT equivalent)

**Other important identities:**
- Double negation: ¬¬P ≡ P
- Idempotence: P ∧ P ≡ P, P ∨ P ≡ P
- Commutativity: P ∧ Q ≡ Q ∧ P, P ∨ Q ≡ Q ∨ P
- Associativity: (P ∧ Q) ∧ R ≡ P ∧ (Q ∧ R)
- Distributivity: P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R)
- Absorption: P ∧ (P ∨ Q) ≡ P, P ∨ (P ∧ Q) ≡ P

These laws collectively form a **Boolean algebra** — the same mathematical structure underpins digital circuit design, where AND/OR/NOT gates implement exactly these operations in silicon.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The truth table generator uses a bitmask to enumerate all 2ⁿ truth-value assignments efficiently. Notice that implication has exactly one false row — when the premise is true and conclusion false. The key result: the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the implication (same output column), but the converse is not. Confusing an implication with its converse is one of the most common logical errors in everyday reasoning.

sections.title: Predicate Logic: Quantifiers and Domains
sections.content:
Propositional logic's weakness is that propositions like 'n is prime' or 'x < y' vary in truth value depending on what n, x, y actually are. **Predicate logic** fixes this by treating such property-statements as **predicates** — functions that take one or more arguments and return a truth value. We write P(x) for 'x satisfies property P', Q(x,y) for 'x and y stand in relation Q', and so on.

Predicate logic adds two **quantifiers**:

**Universal quantifier ∀x P(x)** — 'for all x in the domain, P(x) is true'. To prove ∀x P(x), you must show P holds for an arbitrary, unspecified x. To disprove it, you need a single **counterexample** — one particular x where P fails.

**Existential quantifier ∃x P(x)** — 'there exists at least one x in the domain for which P(x) is true'. To prove ∃x P(x), you give one specific **witness** — a concrete x that makes P true. To disprove it, you must show P fails for every x in the domain.

The **domain of discourse** matters enormously. ∀x (x > 0) is false over the integers (negative numbers exist) but true over the positive integers. Always specify or infer the domain.

**Quantifier negation** (De Morgan's laws for quantifiers):
- ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) — to negate 'all x satisfy P', assert 'some x fails P'
- ¬(∃x P(x)) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x) — to negate 'some x satisfies P', assert 'no x satisfies P'

**Nested quantifiers** are powerful but subtle. ∀x ∃y P(x,y) means 'for every x, there is a y that works (but the y can depend on x)'. ∃y ∀x P(x,y) means 'there is a single y that works for all x simultaneously'. These two are very different! For example: ∀ students ∃ a grade they received is trivially true, but ∃ a grade ∀ students received it would be remarkable.

In programming, ∀x P(x) corresponds to `array.every(P)`, and ∃x P(x) corresponds to `array.some(P)`. The connection between logic and functional programming is not coincidental — formal logic directly inspired languages like Haskell and proof assistants like Coq and Lean.

flowchart TD
    A["Quantifier Statement"] --> B["∀x P(x)\nUniversal"]
    A --> C["∃x P(x)\nExistential"]
    B --> D["To PROVE:\nShow P holds for arbitrary x"]
    B --> E["To DISPROVE:\nFind one counterexample"]
    C --> F["To PROVE:\nExhibit one witness x"]
    C --> G["To DISPROVE:\nShow P fails for all x"]
    D --> H["Negation: ∃x ¬P(x)"]
    F --> I["Negation: ∀x ¬P(x)"]
sections.caption: Proof strategies differ by quantifier. Universal claims require general arguments; existential claims need only one example. Negation flips the quantifier and negates the predicate.

sections.title: Direct Proof: Following the Logic Step by Step
sections.content:
The most natural proof strategy is the **direct proof**: you assume the hypothesis is true and use definitions, axioms, previously proven theorems, and algebraic manipulation to derive the conclusion, step by logical step.

Every step in a direct proof should be justified by citing a definition, an axiom, or a previously established result. This chain of justified steps is what separates a proof from an empirical observation or a lucky guess.

**Example — proving 'if n is odd then n² is odd':**
1. **Assume** n is odd. (Hypothesis)
2. By definition of odd, there exists an integer k such that n = 2k + 1.
3. Compute n² = (2k+1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1.
4. Factor: n² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1.
5. Let m = 2k² + 2k, which is an integer (products and sums of integers are integers).
6. Then n² = 2m + 1, which matches the definition of odd.
7. **Conclude** n² is odd. ∎

Every step is either arithmetic manipulation or appeal to a definition. No hand-waving. Notice that step 2 introduces a **witness** k — this is the existential instantiation of 'n is odd'.

**Example — proving the sum formula 0+1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2 by direct pairing:**
Write the sum S twice — once forwards, once backwards:

S = 0 + 1 + 2 + … + n
S = n + (n-1) + (n-2) + … + 0

Adding column by column: 2S = (n+0) + (1+(n-1)) + … + (n+0) = (n+1) added (n+1) times = (n+1)²... but wait, we have n+1 pairs: 2S = (n+1)(n+1)? No — we have n+1 terms (0 through n), so 2S = (n+1) · (n+1-1+1) = (n+1)·(n+1)? Let us be careful: each pair sums to n+1, and there are n+1 pairs (terms 0 through n), so 2S = (n+1)(n+1)? That gives (n+1)²/2 which is wrong. The correct pairing: pair the k-th term from the start with the k-th from the end — first and last: 0+n = n, next pair: 1+(n-1) = n, each pair sums to n, and there are (n+1)/2 pairs if n is odd... The clean version: 2S = (n+1) × (n+1 terms) is incorrect because each pair contributes once to 2S. Actually: 2S = (n+1)+(n+1)+…+(n+1) with exactly (n+1) copies, giving 2S = (n+1)² — but that is wrong for n=2: sum=3, formula=3, 2×3=6=(2+1)²=9. No. The correct argument: there are n+1 terms (0 through n), each adjacent pair (front+back) sums to n; there are (n+1) such terms contributing to 2S, so 2S = n(n+1)+n — this is getting messy. The cleanest direct proof is Gauss's: 2S = (n+1) repeated (n+1) times... wait: the number of pairs is ⌊(n+1)/2⌋. The elegant statement: pairing the k-th term from each end (0+n, 1+(n-1), etc.) each gives n, and there are (n+1) terms total, so 2S = n(n+1) if n is even, giving S = n(n+1)/2. This holds and generalises to all n ≥ 0 (check n=0: S=0, formula=0; n=1: S=1, formula=1; n=2: S=3, formula=3). The algebraic direct proof is cleaner than the pairing argument — the pairing argument works but requires care about odd/even n. The **induction proof** handles all n uniformly, which is why induction is the preferred technique here.

sections.title: Proof by Contradiction: Ruling Out the Impossible
sections.content:
**Proof by contradiction** (also called *reductio ad absurdum*) works by assuming the negation of what you want to prove and deriving a logical contradiction — a statement that is known to be false, or a pair of statements that cannot both hold. Since sound logical inference from a true starting point cannot produce a false conclusion, the starting point (the negation of your goal) must have been false. Therefore your original goal is true.

The structure is always:
1. **Assume** ¬G (the negation of the goal G).
2. **Derive**, through valid logical steps, some statement C that is false (or two contradictory statements).
3. **Conclude** that ¬G leads to falsehood, so ¬G is false, so G must be true. ∎

**The classic example: √2 is irrational.** (Attributed to ancient Greek mathematicians, possibly Hippasus of Metapontum, circa 5th century BCE.)

*Goal*: √2 is not a rational number — it cannot be expressed as p/q for integers p, q.

1. Assume for contradiction that √2 is rational. Then √2 = p/q where p, q are integers with no common factor (i.e., the fraction is in **lowest terms**).
2. Squaring both sides: 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q².
3. Therefore p² is even (it is 2 times something).
4. Since p² is even, p must be even. (Contrapositive of 'odd × odd = odd', or directly: if p were odd, p = 2k+1, p² = 4k²+4k+1 = odd.)
5. Write p = 2m for some integer m.
6. Substituting back: (2m)² = 2q², so 4m² = 2q², so q² = 2m².
7. Therefore q² is even, so q is even.
8. **Contradiction**: Both p and q are even, meaning both are divisible by 2 — contradicting that p/q was in lowest terms (no common factors).
9. Therefore our assumption was wrong, and √2 is irrational. ∎

This proof has stood for 2500 years. It is also a beautiful demonstration of why **an infinite domain** (all pairs of integers) cannot be handled by checking examples — you cannot list all rational numbers and check each one. The contradiction argument rules out the entire class at once.

**When to reach for contradiction**: contradiction is especially useful when (a) the goal is a negative statement ('there is no largest prime', '√2 is not rational'), (b) the negation gives you rich extra structure to work with, or (c) the direct path is unclear but ruling out the opposite is straightforward.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Goal: Prove G"] --> B["Assume ¬G\n(negation of goal)"]
    B --> C["Apply definitions\nand algebra"]
    C --> D["Derive contradiction C\ne.g. p and q both even\nbut assumed coprime"]
    D --> E["¬G leads to falsehood"]
    E --> F["Therefore ¬G is false"]
    F --> G["Therefore G is TRUE ✓"]
sections.caption: The structure of every proof by contradiction. The contradiction C can be any known falsehood — a violated definition, a previously proven result, or two claims that directly contradict each other.

sections.title: Mathematical Induction: Proving Statements for All Natural Numbers
sections.content:
**Mathematical induction** is the proof technique tailored to statements of the form 'P(n) holds for every natural number n ≥ n₀'. It has two components:

1. **Base case**: Prove P(n₀) directly — usually by substitution and arithmetic.
2. **Inductive step**: Prove that P(k) → P(k+1) for an arbitrary k ≥ n₀. That is, *assume* P(k) is true (this assumption is the **inductive hypothesis**) and *prove* P(k+1) from it.

Why does this work? Think of it as an infinite chain of dominoes. The base case knocks over the first domino. The inductive step says: whenever domino k falls, it topples domino k+1. Therefore every domino falls eventually — P(n) holds for every n.

**Example — proving ∑ᵢ₌₀ⁿ i = n(n+1)/2:**

*Base case* (n=0): LHS = 0. RHS = 0·1/2 = 0. ✓

*Inductive step*: Assume the formula holds for some k ≥ 0 (inductive hypothesis): ∑ᵢ₌₀ᵏ i = k(k+1)/2.

Now prove it for k+1:
∑ᵢ₌₀ᵏ⁺¹ i = (∑ᵢ₌₀ᵏ i) + (k+1)   [separate last term]
= k(k+1)/2 + (k+1)              [apply inductive hypothesis]
= (k+1)(k/2 + 1)                [factor out (k+1)]
= (k+1)(k+2)/2                  [common denominator]
= (k+1)((k+1)+1)/2              [rewrite as formula at n=k+1] ✓

This is the template for every induction proof: write out the (k+1) case, find where to insert the inductive hypothesis (usually by splitting a sum, product, or structure into a 'k part' plus a 'new part'), apply the hypothesis, and simplify to the target form.

**Strong induction** is a variant where the inductive hypothesis is strengthened: instead of assuming only P(k), you assume P(j) for every j with n₀ ≤ j ≤ k. This is logically equivalent to ordinary induction (both prove the same set of statements) but is more convenient when P(k+1) depends on multiple previous values, not just P(k).

**Example requiring strong induction — prime factorization**: Every integer n ≥ 2 can be written as a product of primes.

*Base case* (n=2): 2 is prime, so it is its own factorization. ✓

*Inductive step* (strong): Assume every integer j with 2 ≤ j ≤ k has a prime factorization. Consider n = k+1:
- If k+1 is prime, it is its own factorization. ✓
- If k+1 is composite, then k+1 = a·b where 2 ≤ a, b < k+1. By the inductive hypothesis (applied to both a and b, which are at most k), both a and b have prime factorizations. Combining them gives a prime factorization for k+1. ✓

Notice we needed the hypothesis for *both* a and b, which could be any values from 2 to k — not just k. Ordinary induction (hypothesis only for k) would not suffice here.

**Common mistakes with induction**:
- Forgetting the base case (without it, the chain has no starting point).
- Not using the inductive hypothesis in the inductive step (the step must genuinely depend on it).
- Making the inductive step circular (using what you want to prove).
- Choosing the wrong base case (proofs sometimes require multiple base cases).

flowchart LR
    A["Base Case
Prove P(0) directly"] --> B["Inductive Hypothesis
Assume P(k) is true"]
    B --> C["Inductive Step
Derive P(k+1) from P(k)"]
    C --> D["Chain complete
P(n) for ALL n ≥ 0"]
    E["Strong Induction
Variant"] --> F["Hypothesis:
Assume P(j) for ALL j ≤ k"]

using any P(0)…P(k)"]

sections.caption: Simple induction uses only P(k) to prove P(k+1). Strong induction uses all of P(0) through P(k). Both yield the same conclusion: P holds for all n.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `inductiveStep` function mechanically checks the algebraic identity that the induction proof uses: sumFormula(k) + (k+1) = sumFormula(k+1). This is exactly the step where the inductive hypothesis is applied — replacing the running sum with the closed form, then algebraically simplifying. The √2 irrationality test illustrates why contradiction is needed: no finite enumeration could disprove all rationals, but the symbolic proof rules out every rational at once.

sections.title: Proof by Contrapositive: Flipping the Direction
sections.content:
**Proof by contrapositive** exploits the logical equivalence P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P. Instead of proving 'if P then Q' directly, you prove 'if not Q then not P'. The two statements are logically identical — same truth table — so proving one is sufficient to establish the other.

When is contrapositive easier than direct proof? When the negations ¬Q and ¬P are more tractable than P and Q themselves. Often this happens when P or Q is a negative statement ('n is not divisible by 4', 'the graph has no cycle') that becomes a positive, workable hypothesis after negation.

**Example — proving 'if n² is even then n is even':**

*Direct proof attempt*: Assume n² is even. We need to show n is even. But starting from n² being even and working backwards to n is not obvious — factors do not pull apart easily.

*Contrapositive proof*: Prove the contrapositive: 'if n is not even (i.e., n is odd) then n² is not even (i.e., n² is odd)'.
1. Assume n is odd. Then n = 2k+1 for some integer k.
2. n² = (2k+1)² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1.
3. This has the form 2m+1 (m = 2k²+2k), which is odd. ✓

This is the direct proof of 'n odd → n² odd' that we already showed. By contrapositive equivalence, we have proven 'n² even → n even'. The contrapositive proof feels completely natural here; the direct proof would require working backwards through square roots.

**Contrapositive vs. contradiction**: These are related but different. Contradiction assumes ¬G and derives any falsehood. Contrapositive assumes ¬Q specifically (when the goal is P → Q) and derives ¬P. The contrapositive proof is a *special case* of direct proof — you are proving a direct implication (¬Q → ¬P) — while contradiction is a more general principle. In practice, if you find yourself naturally reaching for contradiction but your assumed negation is just ¬Q and your derived statement is ¬P, you are really doing contrapositive.

flowchart LR
    A["Goal: P → Q"] --> B["Direct Proof
Assume P, derive Q"]
    A --> C["Contrapositive
Assume ¬Q, derive ¬P"]
    A --> D["Contradiction
Assume ¬(P→Q) = P∧¬Q
derive any falsehood"]
    B --> E["Use when P gives
strong structure"]
    C --> F["Use when ¬Q gives
stronger foothold"]
    D --> G["Most general;
uses both P and ¬Q"]
sections.caption: Three proof strategies for the same implication P→Q. The contrapositive is logically equivalent and not a special case of contradiction — it is a different direct proof of the flipped statement.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The nested quantifier example is the key insight: ∀x ∃y means 'for each x, pick a y that works — y can depend on x' (we pick y = -x each time). ∃y ∀x means 'pick one y first, then it must work for all x simultaneously' — clearly impossible since x+y=0 requires y = -x, but x varies. Swapping quantifier order completely changes the meaning of a statement.

sections.content: **Historical context.** Propositional logic was systematised by George Boole in 1847 (giving us 'Boolean algebra') and further developed by Gottlob Frege, who introduced predicate logic in 1879. Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead's *Principia Mathematica* (1910–1913) attempted to derive all of mathematics from logical axioms — a project famously undermined by Kurt Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931), which proved that any sufficiently powerful consistent formal system contains true statements it cannot prove. Despite this, the tools of formal logic became the foundation of computer science: Alan Turing's 1936 computability paper used predicate logic directly, and modern proof assistants like Coq and Lean use dependent type theory — a direct descendant of predicate logic — to verify software correctness.

**Common mistakes and interview insights.** (1) **Converse confusion**: 'If it rains, the street is wet' does NOT imply 'If the street is wet, it rained' — the converse is a separate claim. Confusing P→Q with Q→P is one of the most common logical fallacies in both mathematical proofs and everyday reasoning. (2) **Induction shortcut**: When you see 'prove for all n ≥ k', try induction immediately. The inductive step should use the hypothesis explicitly — if it does not appear, something is wrong. (3) **Counterexamples are cheap**: To disprove a universal claim ∀x P(x), you need exactly one x where P fails. Do not over-engineer a counter-argument. (4) **Contradiction tip**: If the negation of your goal gives you two complementary pieces of structure (like 'p and q are coprime' and 'both are even'), contradiction is probably the right move. (5) **Contrapositive shortcut**: Whenever you see 'if n satisfies property X then n satisfies property Y' and thinking about X directly is hard, negate Y and see if working with ¬Y is more productive.

items: **Propositional logic** uses connectives (¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔) to build compound statements from atomic propositions; truth tables mechanically classify formulas as tautologies, contradictions, or contingencies.
**Implication P→Q** is false in exactly one case — when P is true and Q is false. It is vacuously true whenever P is false. The contrapositive ¬Q→¬P is logically equivalent; the converse Q→P is not.
**De Morgan's laws** (¬(P∧Q) ≡ ¬P∨¬Q and ¬(P∨Q) ≡ ¬P∧¬Q) are the most-used equivalence laws, appearing in proof simplification, programming, and circuit design.

**Predicate logic** adds predicates P(x) and quantifiers ∀ (universal) and ∃ (existential). Negation swaps quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). The order of nested quantifiers ∀x ∃y vs ∃y ∀x fundamentally changes meaning.

**Direct proof** derives the conclusion from the hypothesis step by step. **Proof by contrapositive** proves ¬Q→¬P instead of P→Q (logically equivalent). **Proof by contradiction** assumes ¬G and derives any falsehood.

**Mathematical induction** proves P(n) for all n by: (1) proving P(n₀) directly as the base case, and (2) proving P(k)→P(k+1) using the inductive hypothesis. **Strong induction** assumes all P(j) for j ≤ k and is needed when P(k+1) depends on multiple predecessors.

Proof technique selection is guided by the statement's form: universal claims about naturals → induction; negative goals ('no such x exists') → contradiction; hard forward direction → try contrapositive; structured hypothesis → direct proof.

quiz.question: The implication P → Q is false in exactly which case?
options: When both P and Q are false
When P is false and Q is true
When P is true and Q is false
When both P and Q are true
quiz.explanation: Implication represents a promise 'if P then Q'. The promise is broken — the implication is false — only when P is true (we committed) and Q is false (we failed to deliver). When P is false, no commitment was made, so the implication is vacuously true regardless of Q.

quiz.question: Which statement is logically equivalent to P → Q?
options: Q → P (the converse)
¬P → ¬Q (the inverse)
¬Q → ¬P (the contrapositive)
P ∧ ¬Q
quiz.explanation: The contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P has exactly the same truth table as P → Q — they are logically equivalent. The converse Q → P and inverse ¬P → ¬Q are equivalent to each other but NOT to the original implication. Confusing an implication with its converse is a classic logical fallacy.

quiz.question: What does De Morgan's law state about ¬(P ∧ Q)?
options: ¬P ∧ ¬Q
¬P ∨ ¬Q
P ∨ ¬Q
¬P ∧ Q
quiz.explanation: De Morgan's law: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Negating an AND flips it to OR of the negations. The companion law: ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q — negating an OR gives AND of negations. The mnemonic: push negation through a connective and the connective flips.

quiz.question: In proof by mathematical induction, what exactly must the inductive step prove?
options: That P(0) holds for the specific base case
That P(k) is true for every specific integer k ≥ 0
That assuming P(k) implies P(k+1) for an arbitrary k
That the statement holds for the largest possible n
quiz.explanation: The inductive step proves the implication P(k) → P(k+1) for an arbitrary k ≥ n₀. You assume P(k) as the inductive hypothesis — you do not prove P(k) in this step. The base case handles P(n₀), and the chain P(n₀)→P(n₀+1)→… then establishes P(n) for all n ≥ n₀.

quiz.question: What is the negation of the statement ∀x P(x)?
options: ∀x ¬P(x)
∃x ¬P(x)
∃x P(x)
quiz.explanation: ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). To disprove 'every x satisfies P', you only need one counterexample — an x for which P fails. Similarly, ¬(∃x P(x)) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x): to disprove 'some x satisfies P', you must show P fails for all x.

quiz.question: How many rows does a truth table for 4 propositional variables require?
quiz.explanation: A truth table for n variables needs 2ⁿ rows to cover every combination of true/false assignments. For n=4: 2⁴ = 16 rows. This exponential growth is why truth tables are impractical for large n — SAT solvers use backtracking and heuristics instead.

quiz.question: In the classic proof that √2 is irrational, what contradiction is reached?
options: A number is shown to be both positive and negative
p and q are both proven even, contradicting that p/q was in lowest terms
√2 is shown to equal both 1 and 2
The assumption implies 2 = 1
quiz.explanation: The proof assumes √2 = p/q in lowest terms (no common factors), then derives p² = 2q², showing p is even (p = 2m), substituting back to get q² = 2m², showing q is also even. Both p and q being even means they share factor 2, contradicting the assumption that p/q was in lowest terms.

quiz.question: A tautology is a propositional formula that is:
options: True for exactly half of all variable assignments
True for at least one variable assignment
True for all possible variable assignments
False for all possible variable assignments
quiz.explanation: A tautology is true in every row of its truth table, regardless of variable assignments. Classic examples: P ∨ ¬P (law of excluded middle), and (P → Q) → (¬Q → ¬P) (contrapositive law). A formula true for at least one assignment is satisfiable; false for all assignments is a contradiction.

quiz.question: Strong induction differs from simple induction in that the inductive hypothesis:
options: Assumes only P(k-1) instead of P(k)
Assumes P(0), P(1), …, P(k) all hold when proving P(k+1)
Requires proving two explicit base cases instead of one
Can only be applied to statements about even numbers
quiz.explanation: In strong (complete) induction, you assume P(j) holds for ALL j with n₀ ≤ j ≤ k when proving P(k+1), not just P(k). This is needed when P(k+1) depends on multiple predecessors — for example, proving every integer ≥ 2 has a prime factorization requires knowing the result for all integers from 2 to k, not only k.

quiz.question: Why does the proof strategy differ between proving ∀x P(x) and proving ∃x P(x)?
options: Universal proofs always use induction; existential proofs always use contradiction
Universal proofs require showing P holds for an arbitrary x; existential proofs need only one concrete witness
Existential proofs are always harder than universal proofs
Both require checking all elements of the domain
quiz.explanation: To prove ∀x P(x), you must show P holds for a completely arbitrary x (no special assumptions about x) — this general argument covers the entire domain. To prove ∃x P(x), you only need to exhibit one concrete x (a 'witness') for which P is true. This asymmetry is fundamental: disproving ∀ needs one counterexample, but disproving ∃ requires ruling out all candidates.
